summary.text: Bird migration is the seasonal movement of some birds between breeding and wintering grounds, twice a year and usually between northern and southern regions.
Food seems to be the main motive, and the long days of the northern summer give breeding birds extra time to feed their young.
Timing seems to be controlled mainly by day length, and migrating birds find their way using the Sun, stars, the Earth's magnetic field and mental maps.

items.prompt: A householder keeps hummingbird feeders full all winter, and some birds that would normally leave stay. What does that suggest about the cause of migration?

options.label: Cold weather alone is the main driver
Finding enough to eat appears to be the main motivation
Predators in the north force birds out
Nest sites run out in winter

items.explain: The primary motivation for migration appears to be food; some hummingbirds choose not to migrate if fed through the winter.

items.prompt: Populations that nest farthest north winter farthest south, jumping over populations that nest nearer the south. What is this called?

options.label: Chain migration
Partial migration
Nomadism
Leap-frog migration

items.explain: In leap-frog migration, birds that nest at higher latitudes spend the winter at lower latitudes, bypassing sedentary populations.

items.prompt: A falcon on Mediterranean islands waits until autumn to raise its chicks. What is the likely reason?

options.label: Its chicks are fed on small birds passing south on migration then
Summer heat on the islands is too fierce for chicks
Autumn is when the islands' own birds nest
It waits for the Mediterranean sea to cool

items.explain: Eleonora's falcon breeds very late, coordinated with the autumn passage of southbound passerine migrants, which it feeds to its young.

items.prompt: Birds heading south spread out at first, then many squeeze into a few corridors along mountains and coasts. What might help them?

options.label: Such corridors can offer updrafts and winds and avoid wide open water
Narrow corridors keep different species apart so they cannot compete
Every bird follows one fixed route out and back each year
Birds prefer land because they cannot steer by stars over water

items.explain: Flyways often follow mountain ranges or coastlines and may take advantage of updrafts and wind patterns or avoid geographical barriers such as large stretches of open water.

items.prompt: A bird that flies north to breed lays more eggs than a close relative living year-round in the tropics. What advantage helps?

options.label: Northern nests face no predators at all
Tropical days are too short to raise young
Long northern summer days give parents extra time to feed the young
The warm northern summer makes eggs hatch faster

items.explain: The longer days of the northern summer give breeding birds extended time to feed their young, helping diurnal birds produce larger clutches than related non-migratory species in the tropics.

items.prompt: In 1822 a white stork was found in Germany with an arrow made of central African hardwood. What did that suggest?

options.label: Storks had been carried north by people on long boat trips
Storks can travel from central Africa to Europe on long migrations
Storks spend their winters under water, like swallows
Storks stay in one area all year round, wherever they hatch

items.explain: The Pfeilstorch provided some of the earliest evidence of long-distance stork migration.

paragraphs.heading: What migration is
paragraphs.text: Bird migration is the seasonal movement of some birds, twice a year, between the places where they breed and the places where they spend the winter, usually between north and south. It is marked by its yearly rhythm and by travel between breeding and non-breeding areas. Birds that do not migrate are called resident or sedentary. Of the roughly 10,000 bird species in the world, about 1,800 migrate long distances.

paragraphs.heading: What does not count
paragraphs.text: Not every movement is migration. Moves made in response to changes in food, habitat or weather are not, and irregular trips such as invasions and irruptions, or one-way moves such as young birds dispersing from where they hatched, are not called true migration either. Short migrations are common and long ones are not. The short kind includes moving up and down mountains such as the Andes and Himalayas.

paragraphs.heading: Why birds go
paragraphs.text: The commonest pattern is to fly north in spring to breed in the temperate or Arctic summer, then return in autumn to warmer wintering grounds to the south. In the southern hemisphere the directions are reversed, though there is less land far south to support long-distance migration. Food appears to be the main reason: some hummingbirds skip migration if they are fed through the winter. Long northern summer days give parents more time to feed their young, which helps daytime birds raise bigger clutches than related species that stay in the tropics. These gains outweigh the stress, effort and risks of the trip.

paragraphs.heading: Timing and finding the way
paragraphs.text: Changes in day length seem to be the main signal that sets when birds go. To find their way, migrating birds rely on mental maps, the Earth's magnetic field, and cues from the Sun and stars. Most migrations start on a broad front that often narrows into favoured routes called flyways. These usually follow mountain ranges, coastlines or sometimes rivers, may use updrafts and other winds, and avoid barriers such as wide stretches of open water. A route can be learned or inherited in the genes, to different degrees, and the way out often differs from the way back.

paragraphs.heading: Different patterns
paragraphs.text: Not every population of a species has to migrate, which is called partial migration; in Australia 44% of non-passerine and 32% of passerine species are partially migratory. In some species, populations at higher latitudes fly past areas where others of their kind stay all year and winter at lower latitudes, which is leap-frog migration. In chain migration, by contrast, populations slide north and south more evenly without changing order. Ages and sexes can differ too: female chaffinches in eastern Fennoscandia leave earlier in autumn than males, and European tits migrate only in their first year.

paragraphs.heading: Records and dangers
paragraphs.text: The Arctic tern holds the distance record, travelling each year between Arctic breeding grounds and the Antarctic. Manx shearwaters cover 14,000 km between northern breeding sites and the Southern Ocean, and some albatrosses circle the Earth over southern seas. The trip is risky. Eleonora's falcon has a very late breeding season on Mediterranean islands, timed to the autumn passage of southbound passerine migrants that it feeds to its young, and the greater noctule bat preys on passerines migrating at night. Crowding at stopover sites also exposes birds to parasites and pathogens.

paragraphs.heading: An arrow in a stork
paragraphs.text: In 1822 a white stork turned up in the German state of Mecklenburg carrying an arrow made from central African hardwood. It gave some of the earliest evidence that storks migrate long distances, and the bird became known as the Pfeilstorch, German for arrow stork. People had noticed migration long before: in the Pacific, the land-finding methods of Micronesians and Polynesians suggest birds were watched and interpreted for more than 3,000 years.
